command: smoke, overloaded host, not a benchmark result

podman.network: one private bridge network per run; each engine is published only on an ephemeral 127.0.0.1 port

shape.id: document ID, 'doc-' plus 8 zero-padded digits; Yamora path name, MongoDB _id, PostgreSQL primary key column
shape.tags: array of 3 distinct strings from t000..t255
shape.attributes: map of color (string), size (string) and weight_g (integer)
shape.description: 32-56 lowercase ASCII words drawn uniformly from a 1024-word vocabulary (text indexed)
shape.yaml_comment: Yamora's YAML source starts with one comment line; MongoDB and PostgreSQL receive the same values as JSON without it

settings.name: smoke
settings.engine_order: rotated by one position per repetition
settings.timing: monotonic clock per request inside each client process; phase throughput is requests over the span from the first worker's start to the last worker's end; ingest and delete use the summed time inside their batch calls

yamora.version: 0.3.0 (Python package version; daemon from this checkout)

build.source: built from this checkout with the Makefile defaults

yamora.runtime: podman --rootfs: the built binary plus its host shared libraries
yamora.durability: Native disk engine default (not configurable): each commit writes its records and copy-on-write tree pages, synchronizes, writes the alternate superblock and synchronizes again before replying.
yamora.cache: --cache-bytes 268435456 (tree pages only; records use the OS page cache)
yamora.client: yamora.YamoraClient (Python standard library, HTTP/1.1 JSON, new TCP connection per request)

mongodb.durability: WiredTiger journal on (always enabled since MongoDB 6.1); every insert, update and delete uses writeConcern {w: 1, j: true}, which waits for the journal flush.
mongodb.client: yamora.benchmarks.compare.mongo_wire (Python standard library OP_MSG/BSON/SCRAM-SHA-256; one persistent TCP connection per client process; not the official driver)

postgresql.schema: items(id text PRIMARY KEY, doc jsonb NOT NULL); B-tree expression indexes on doc->'category' and doc->'price'; GIN on to_tsvector('simple', doc->>'description')
postgresql.durability: fsync=on, synchronous_commit=on, full_page_writes=on, wal_sync_method=fdatasync; every statement autocommits, so each insert batch, update and delete batch waits for its WAL flush.
postgresql.cache: shared_buffers=256MB, plus the OS page cache inside the container limit
postgresql.client: psycopg2 (C extension over libpq; one persistent connection per client process); psycopg2 2.9.12

text.method: native inverted postings (search API reports work counters)

memory.method: cgroup.procs sampled every 0.25s; VmRSS and smaps_rollup Pss summed; cgroup memory.peak
cgroup.procs sampled every 0.25s; VmRSS and smaps_rollup Pss summed; cgroup memory.peak

eq.plan: Limit > Bitmap Heap Scan > Bitmap Index Scan(items_category)

range.plan: Limit > Sort > Bitmap Heap Scan > Bitmap Index Scan(items_price)

memory.method: cgroup.procs sampled every 0.25s; VmRSS and smaps_rollup Pss summed; cgroup memory.peak

caveats: Results describe only this workload, dataset, machine and configuration; they are not a general ranking of the engines.

Transport differs: YamoraDB is measured over HTTP/1.1 with JSON request envelopes and a new TCP connection per request (its Python client's behavior); MongoDB uses its binary OP_MSG wire protocol and PostgreSQL its frontend/backend protocol, each over one persistent connection per client process. Yamora's TLS-only binary listener was not used.

Client implementations differ: YamoraDB uses its pure-Python standard-library client, MongoDB a pure-Python OP_MSG/BSON client written for this harness (not the official driver; no C-accelerated BSON), and PostgreSQL psycopg2, a C extension over libpq.
Point reads return different representations: YamoraDB returns exact YAML bytes without parsing them; MongoDB and PostgreSQL clients decode BSON or JSONB into Python objects.

Caches were set to 256 MiB each but cover different things: Yamora's tree-page cache excludes records, WiredTiger's cache holds uncompressed pages, and PostgreSQL's shared_buffers double-buffers with the OS page cache. All three also use the OS page cache charged to their 1 GiB container memory limit.

Durability was matched as closely as each engine allows: Yamora synchronizes every commit twice (records, then superblock); MongoDB waits for its journal (w:1, j:true); PostgreSQL waits for its WAL flush (synchronous_commit=on). The mechanisms and the number of synchronizations per commit differ.

Text search compares single-term lookups returning any 20 matches. Ordering and scoring differ (Yamora: document-ID order, matched-term count; MongoDB: unspecified order without a score sort; PostgreSQL: unspecified order); no relevance ranking is compared. Stemming and stop words are disabled on all three (Yamora has none, MongoDB default_language none, PostgreSQL the simple configuration).

PostgreSQL runs ANALYZE once after the bulk load (standard practice); the other engines have no equivalent step. Disk sizes are measured after an explicit checkpoint (MongoDB fsync, PostgreSQL CHECKPOINT; Yamora needs none) and without compaction, VACUUM FULL or MongoDB compact, so space freed by deletes is generally not returned.

On-disk size is st_blocks-allocated bytes of each data directory, including journals, WAL and diagnostics. Filesystem compression or copy-on-write (for example btrfs) can make physical usage differ from these figures; MongoDB also compresses blocks (snappy) by default while Yamora and PostgreSQL (below the TOAST threshold) do not.

Peak memory is sampled every 0.25 s: summed RSS counts shared memory once per process (overstating multi-process PostgreSQL), summed PSS divides it, and cgroup memory.peak includes page cache charged to the container.

YamoraDB additionally guarantees exact YAML source preservation: raw reads return the stored bytes, comments and formatting included, and the harness verifies this. MongoDB and PostgreSQL store parsed values and do not keep the source text.

YamoraDB lacks capabilities the others have, including a production-qualified replication/HA profile (its replica-set profile is experimental), relevance-ranked text search with stemming or phrases, and persistent connections in its Python client; this workload measures none of those capabilities.

All engines ran in Podman with --cpus 2 and --memory/--memory-swap 1g on one private network, published only on 127.0.0.1, on the same filesystem; the benchmark client processes ran on the host without CPU limits. Engines ran one at a time, never concurrently, in an order rotated per repetition.
